records.sourceFile: Association between sports injuries and sleep as measured by sleep actigraphy - A scoping review.pdf

paper.citation: Lytle C, Krishnan P, Saraf SM, Mulcahey MK. Association between sports injuries and sleep as measured by sleep actigraphy: a scoping review. The Physician and Sportsmedicine. 2026. Accepted author version, online 31 January 2026.
paper.abstract: This scoping review mapped studies that used wrist actigraphy to examine sleep in relation to sports injuries and athletic performance. Among 17 studies with 455 athletes, injury findings were mixed, while all eight performance studies linked poorer sleep metrics to worse performance, with aerobic and reaction-time measures most consistently affected.
paper.tldr: Wrist actigraphy studies in athletes link poorer sleep to worse performance, most consistently aerobic and reaction-time measures. The evidence that poor sleep raises injury risk is inconclusive, and the small, varied sample limits firm conclusions.
paper.methods: Scoping review following the PRISMA-ScR checklist. PubMed, Medline, Embase and SPORTDiscus were searched in January 2024 and updated in January 2025 for peer-reviewed English-language studies, published within 24 years, that used sleep actigraphy and reported injury or athletic performance outcomes. Concussion studies, reviews and studies using questionnaires or other sleep measures were excluded; two authors screened abstracts and full texts, and no formal risk-of-bias appraisal was performed.
paper.findings: Of seven injury studies, four (57%) found poorer sleep metrics (longer sleep onset latency, more wake after sleep onset, lower sleep efficiency) associated with more injuries, in Paralympic, adolescent track and field and elite soccer athletes, while three (43%) found no association with sleep duration or efficiency. All eight performance studies (47% of the 17 included) found poorer sleep associated with worse performance, including aerobic capacity, race or time-trial times and reaction time; sprint and sport-specific accuracy findings were mixed.
paper.limitations: The conclusion states that no significant relationship was found between sleep and injury rates in adult athletes, but the results report significant associations in adult elite soccer players (two studies, one a single-athlete case study) and Paralympic athletes; the abstract's 'no consensus' wording fits the results better. The review did not appraise study quality, included only seven injury studies with small samples (1 to 94 athletes), and had 23% female participants; its statement that actigraphy is reliable was not tested by the review.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff can use wrist actigraphy to track sleep duration, latency and efficiency alongside performance testing, since the included studies connect those metrics to aerobic and reaction-time results. Staff should not treat poor sleep as a proven injury risk factor for adult athletes, and should record recent sleep when interpreting a weak aerobic or reaction-time result.
paper.athleteDev: In the included studies, poorer sleep metrics were associated with worse aerobic performance, reaction time and some anaerobic tests, so sleep monitoring can sit alongside performance testing. The review cannot show that improving sleep causes better performance, and the anaerobic and sprint findings are mixed.
paper.rtp: Not designed for return to sport. The review does not study injured athletes or recovery after injury, and it describes the injury link as inconclusive, so it cannot be used to set sleep criteria for return to training or competition.

records.sourceFile: Baseline sleep characteristics in NCAA Division 1 collegiate athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Goldman JT, Donohoe B, Hatamiya N, Boland NF, Vail J, Holmes KE, et al. Baseline Sleep Characteristics in NCAA Division I Collegiate Athletes. Clin J Sport Med. 2024.
paper.abstract: This prospective study measured baseline sleep in 82 Division I collegiate athletes using a wearable sleep device worn for at least 14 nights, plus two validated sleep questionnaires. Total sleep time averaged about 6.8 hours with no sex difference, and men had longer wake time after sleep onset than women. Sleep architecture, sleep consistency and questionnaire scores did not differ by sex.
paper.tldr: Division I athletes at one university averaged about 6.8 hours of wearable-measured sleep, with no sex difference in total sleep, sleep stages or consistency. Men had about 11 more minutes of wake time after sleep onset than women.
paper.methods: Prospective study of varsity athletes from nine teams at one Division I university, who wore a WHOOP 4.0 band for at least 14 nights (average 67.7 days of data) and completed the Epworth Sleepiness Scale and Single-Item Sleep Quality Scale. Men and women were compared with t tests or Wilcoxon rank sum tests at a significance level of 0.05, with no multiple-comparison correction reported.
paper.findings: Mean total sleep time was 409.2 +/- 36.3 minutes, with no sex difference (403.8 vs 416.5 minutes, P = 0.215). Average wake time after sleep onset was 50.2 +/- 16.2 minutes and was longer in men (55.0 vs 43.7 minutes, P = 0.020). Sleep stages (REM 25.6%, slow-wave 19.9%, light 54.4%), sleep consistency (61.6 +/- 8.9%), Single-Item Sleep Quality Scale scores (6.48 +/- 1.71) and Epworth scores (7.57 +/- 3.82) did not differ significantly by sex.
paper.limitations: The study was supported by grant funding from WHOOP, Inc., and three authors are WHOOP employees, although the article states the authors report no conflicts of interest. Data were collected at varying times of the year without accounting for competition or academic schedules, the sport groups are small and unequal, and the wake-time result was not corrected for multiple comparisons. The questionnaires were validated in the general population, not in athletes, and the authors' conclusion that many athletes sleep less than 6 hours and that sleep optimization improves performance goes beyond the data reported.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff can use about 6.8 hours of total sleep and about 50 minutes of wake time after sleep onset as a reference for this group of athletes. The study does not show whether these values are a problem or how they relate to performance, injury or illness, so an individual's own trend matters more than the group average.
paper.athleteDev: Wearable sleep data gave this group a baseline for sleep duration, stages and consistency that staff can compare with an individual athlete's own trend. The study did not link sleep to performance, so it cannot justify a performance-based sleep target.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return-to-sport decisions. It describes baseline sleep in varsity athletes and does not measure sleep after injury or any link between sleep and recovery from injury.

records.sourceFile: Blood Flow Restricted Electrical Stimulations to Prevent or Attenuate Symptoms of Muscle Damage.pdf

paper.citation: Cintron HE, Heyburn JJ, Sterner RL, Dankel SJ. Blood Flow Restricted Electrical Stimulations to Prevent or Attenuate Symptoms of Muscle Damage. Research in Sports Medicine. 2022.
paper.abstract: Eighteen participants completed a damaging eccentric exercise bout with both arms, followed by electrical stimulation with or without blood flow restriction on each arm, repeated 24 hours later. Discomfort, muscle thickness and strength changed over time after the damaging exercise, but the two treatment conditions did not differ.
paper.tldr: Adding blood flow restriction to low-frequency electrical stimulation did not reduce soreness, strength loss or swelling after an eccentric arm exercise bout. The study had no control arm and used one muscle group, so it cannot show that either treatment works.
paper.methods: Within-subject design. Eighteen participants (9 female, 9 male; 21 years, 170 cm, 78 kg) performed eccentric elbow flexion to failure at 80% of concentric 1RM with both arms. One arm then received 20 minutes of 5 Hz electrical stimulation alone, and the other the same stimulation with the cuff inflated to 100% of arterial occlusion pressure in 2-minute bouts with 1-minute rests, with conditions counterbalanced for limb dominance. Treatments were given immediately and 24 hours after the exercise; discomfort (Borg CR10), isometric strength and ultrasound muscle thickness were analysed with Bayesian repeated-measures ANOVA.
paper.findings: Eccentric exercise produced clear time effects: discomfort rose from 0 to 4.2 au at 48 h, muscle thickness from 3.5 to 3.8 cm, and isometric strength fell from 278 N to 232 N, with strength lower at both 24 h and 48 h. There was no condition by time interaction on any outcome (BF10 0.154 to 0.279). Condition main effects were absent for strength (BF10 0.208, moderate support for no difference) and muscle thickness (BF10 0.388, inconclusive by the authors' thresholds).
paper.limitations: There was no control condition and no BFR-only condition, so the design cannot separate treatment effects from the natural course of muscle damage. The abstract states all Bayes factors were below 0.28, but the results report BF10 0.388 for the muscle thickness condition effect. The authors also note that the results may depend on the specific stimulation and BFR protocols and on timing, since both were applied at 0 and 24 h only.
paper.practicalImplications: On this evidence, do not add blood flow restriction to low-frequency electrical stimulation expecting less soreness or strength loss after heavy eccentric arm work. The study also cannot show that either treatment beats doing nothing, so it does not support using either one for recovery planning.
paper.athleteDev: The study gives no support for using blood flow restriction with electrical stimulation to speed recovery of strength or readiness after heavy eccentric work. Athletic status was not reported, so any performance use would need separate testing in trained athletes.
paper.rtp: Not applicable. The participants were uninjured and the study measured no injured muscle or return-to-sport outcome.

records.sourceFile: Brief cycles of lower limb occlusion accelerate recovery kinetics in soccer players.pdf

paper.citation: Daab W, Bouzid MA, Lajri M, Bouchiba M, Rebai H. Brief cycles of lower-limb occlusion accelerate recovery kinetics in soccer players. The Physician and Sportsmedicine. 2020.
paper.abstract: Twelve male semiprofessional soccer players completed a simulated match (Loughborough Intermittent Shuttle Test) in a placebo-controlled crossover design, with intermittent lower-limb occlusion (IVO) or low-pressure placebo applied afterwards. Compared with placebo, IVO was associated with better maintained MVC and 20 m sprint over 48 hours, lower soreness, and lower CK at 0 and 24 h; jump results did not differ significantly between conditions.
paper.tldr: In semiprofessional soccer players, brief intermittent occlusion after a simulated match was followed by less soreness, lower CK at 0 and 24 h, and better maintained MVC and sprint than placebo, but not significantly different jump recovery. The sample was small and players were not blinded, so this is an early signal rather than settled evidence.
paper.methods: Single-blind, placebo-randomized crossover with two sessions a week apart. Players did the Loughborough Intermittent Shuttle Test; then IVO (three 5-minute occlusions with 5-minute reperfusion, cuff on the proximal thigh at 50 mmHg above systolic) or placebo (20 mmHg) was applied. MVC, squat jump, countermovement jump, 20 m sprint, CK, LDH, CRP and soreness were measured before, immediately after, and at 24, 48 and 72 h.
paper.findings: Compared with placebo, IVO gave higher MVC at 0, 24 and 48 h and faster 20 m sprints at 24 and 48 h (significant condition by time interactions). For squat jump and countermovement jump there was no significant condition by time interaction (p = 0.06 and p = 0.15), although jumps fell only in the placebo condition on within-condition tests. CK was lower with IVO at 0 and 24 h, LDH at 0 h only, and soreness at 0 and 24 h; CRP did not differ between conditions.
paper.limitations: Only 12 players from one team, with no non-cuff control, and participants could not be blinded because of the obvious cuff pressure difference. Sprint (ICC 0.69, CV 11.2%) and CK (ICC 0.70) reliability were low. The abstract states that IVO attenuated jump decrements and lowered LDH over recovery, but the results show no significant interaction for jumps and an LDH difference only at 0 h.
paper.practicalImplications: For squads playing frequent matches, IVO after a match-like session may be a practical recovery option at the pressures used here (three 5-minute cycles, 50 mmHg above systolic). The benefit was limited to some time points and was tested once in a small group. Monitor CK, soreness and jump or sprint tests to see whether it helps your own players.
paper.athleteDev: Performance staff can note that IVO after a simulated match was associated with less soreness and with MVC and 20 m sprint closer to baseline over 48 hours, while jump recovery did not differ significantly from placebo. If repeating the approach, use a similar test battery and note that sprint and CK reliability were low in this study.
paper.rtp: Not applicable. Players were healthy and no injury or return-to-play outcomes were measured. The study covers short-term recovery of function after a simulated match in uninjured athletes and cannot inform return to sport after injury.

records.sourceFile: Can We Trust Them - An Expert Evaluation of Large Language Models to Provide Sleep and Jet Lag Recommendations for Athletes.pdf

paper.citation: Vitale J, McCall A, Cina A, Athlete Travel and Sleep Interest Group (ATSIG), Janse van Rensburg DC, Halson S. "Can we trust them?" An expert evaluation of large language models to provide sleep and jet lag recommendations for athletes. Sports Medicine. 2025.
paper.abstract: Expert evaluation of sleep and jet lag advice from three large language models (ChatGPT-3.5, ChatGPT-4 and Google Bard) for athletes, using 10 frequently asked questions per topic and 20 experts rating answers at two time points. Sleep answers were largely rated valid with no significant differences between models, while jet lag answers were valid only for ChatGPT-4 and Google Bard was rated lowest, and inter-rater reliability was low while intra-rater agreement was high.
paper.tldr: Experts judged most large language model sleep answers for athletes to be appropriate, but jet lag answers were mostly not, and only ChatGPT-4's jet lag answers passed the content validity threshold overall. Experts disagreed substantially on what counted as appropriate, so model output needs expert review before use.
paper.methods: Ten sleep and ten jet lag FAQs were chosen by three investigators, with ChatGPT-4 also suggesting questions. The three models answered each question on 25 January 2024 with a 150-word instruction, and 20 experts, blinded to model, rated each answer on a 6-point scale with reasons for inappropriate answers, at two time points 8 weeks apart. Lawshe's content validity ratio treated scores of 4 to 6 as appropriate, with Fleiss' kappa for inter-rater reliability, the Jaccard index for intra-rater agreement, and Friedman, ANOVA and chi-square tests for model differences.
paper.findings: Sleep: CVR was 0.5 or higher for 70%, 60% and 90% of answers from ChatGPT-3.5, Google Bard and ChatGPT-4, with no significant differences between models in sleep CVR. Jet lag: ChatGPT-4 answers were all valid (CVI 0.68), ChatGPT-3.5 reached validity on 10% and Google Bard on none, with Google Bard lower than ChatGPT-3.5 (p = 0.0073) and ChatGPT-4 (p < 0.0001) and ChatGPT-4 higher than ChatGPT-3.5 (p = 0.0017). Inter-rater reliability was low (Fleiss' kappa 0.17 to 0.26), while at least 52.6% of experts reached a Jaccard index of 0.76 or more for each model; for jet lag, 'too few information' was the most common criticism (Google Bard 39%), and Google Bard drew the most 'clear mistakes' ratings (21%).
paper.limitations: Small expert panel of 20 with low inter-rater agreement, no athlete or coach raters, and models tested in one period, so results may not hold for current versions. The abstract's Fleiss' kappa range (0.21 to 0.39) does not match Table 3 (0.17 to 0.26). The authors could not calculate an ICC, and the study did not test whether the advice changed athlete outcomes. The Key Points and Conclusion say ChatGPT-4 was consistently better on sleep, but sleep CVR did not differ significantly between models.
paper.practicalImplications: Use language models only as a starting point for athlete sleep and jet lag advice, and have a qualified staff member check the content before passing it on. Expect weaker answers on jet lag than on sleep, and check sleep answers for generic content, since experts' open comments on sleep answers flagged generic wording and missing sport-specific context.
paper.athleteDev: Staff who use a language model to draft sleep or travel guidance should check each answer against their own sport-specific evidence before it goes to athletes or coaches. The models gave different advice on jet lag, and experts disagreed among themselves, so a single model answer should not set a travel plan.
paper.rtp: This study cannot inform return to sport. It assessed general sleep and jet lag advice for athletes and did not test injured athletes or return-to-play decisions.

records.sourceFile: Cannabis use for exercise recovery in trained individuals - A survey study.pdf

paper.citation: Pinzone AG, Erb EK, Humm SM, Kearney SG, Kingsley JD. Cannabis use for exercise recovery in trained individuals: a survey study. Journal of Cannabis Research. 2023;5:32.
paper.abstract: This survey asked 111 regular cannabis users who also exercised whether they used CBD or THC to recover from aerobic or resistance exercise, and what other recovery methods they used. Most respondents trained aerobically or with resistance and most felt that cannabis helped their recovery. The authors conclude that the role of cannabis in exercise recovery needs more data.
paper.tldr: Regular cannabis users who exercise widely believe CBD or THC helps their recovery, but this was a self-report survey with no objective recovery measures or control group. It shows how exercisers use cannabis, not whether it works.
paper.methods: Voluntary, anonymous online questionnaire ('Cannabis and Exercise') advertised on social media, by word of mouth and by flyer, collected June to November 2022. Eligible respondents were at least 18, currently using cannabis and exercising regularly; items covered cannabis use, exercise habits, recovery methods and demographics. Analysis used Kruskal-Wallis tests, chi-square tests and Pearson correlations.
paper.findings: Of 111 respondents, 85% reported aerobic training, 85% resistance training and 72% both. Respondents reported using THC after aerobic exercise (68 people, 61%) or resistance exercise (67 people, 60%) for recovery, and 22 (20%) and 25 (23%) used CBD for each. The authors report that 93% felt CBD and 87% felt THC aided recovery, and found no significant correlation between motives for use and reported recovery.
paper.limitations: The survey is anonymous, voluntary and self-reported, so it measures belief and use rather than recovery, and it has no control group; the authors call it exploratory with a small, mostly Midwest US sample. Reported counts do not reconcile (85% of 111 trained aerobically, yet n = 72 is used; 22 used CBD for recovery but only 20 are CBD users), and the Discussion says women CBD users had higher aerobic intensity while the Results and Table 2 show the difference for resistance exercise. The study asked whether respondents exercised with a team but does not report competition level, so it cannot be read as an athlete sample.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff should expect athletes who train regularly to raise cannabis as a recovery aid and should ask about the product, form and timing they use; respondents reported both CBD and THC use after training, and some reported negative effects such as feeling too high, too sleepy or a racing heart. Because the evidence here is perceived benefit only, staff should not present cannabis as a proven recovery aid.
paper.athleteDev: The survey shows that regular exercisers use CBD and THC as a recovery aid, and men CBD users reported higher aerobic and resistance training intensity, and women CBD users higher resistance intensity, than THC users. It does not measure performance or recovery, so it cannot show that cannabis improves training output.
paper.rtp: The survey does not measure injury, pain, return to sport or clinical recovery, although pain relief was one of the stated motives. It should not be used to guide return-to-play, medication or clearance decisions for an injured athlete.

records.sourceFile: Causes of sleep deprivation in competative athletes - A scoping review.pdf

paper.citation: Pradzynska M, Rylands LP, Canham DC. Causes of sleep deprivation in competative athletes: A scoping review. Science & Sports. 2023.
paper.abstract: This scoping review aimed to identify themes in peer-reviewed studies related to possible causes of sleep deprivation in competitive athletes. Following PRISMA-ScR guidance and searches of PubMed, MEDLINE and EBSCO, 16 studies were included. Five themes were identified, covering travel, night performance, the period before, during and after competition, and concussion, with short-term and long-term causes separated.
paper.tldr: A review of 16 studies found that travel, late-night training or matches, and competition periods were linked to shorter or poorer sleep in athletes, and that concussion history was linked to insomnia. The included studies show associations, so the causes are not proven.
paper.methods: Scoping review following PRISMA-ScR, using three databases searched for 2015 to 2022 with keywords on athletes, sleep and sport. Titles and abstracts were screened, and full texts were checked for eligibility, which required English-language, peer-reviewed, primary studies in athletes that addressed causes of sleep disturbance. Qualitative, quantitative and mixed-method studies were eligible, and reviews were excluded.
paper.findings: Short-term causes: five studies linked long-haul travel, sleeping on the bus or unfamiliar environments to poorer sleep or more fatigue, although one triathlon study reported no change in sleep quality and an increase in sleep duration after long-haul travel; all four night-performance studies showed at least one significant change in sleep quality or quantity after night training or matches. Around competition, one study of professional rugby players reported a 68% sleep efficiency on the night of competition, and 64% of athletes in another study reported worse sleep on at least one night before an important competition, while a cricket study found no change in pre-competition sleep. Long-term causes: a history of concussion was associated with a higher risk of moderate to severe insomnia (P = 0.006) and with short sleep and sleep disturbance across three studies.
paper.limitations: The review did not assess the quality or risk of bias of the included studies, and it covers only English-language studies from 2015 to 2022 in three databases. Most included designs are observational, and the review's own conclusion is that it is a starting point rather than a definitive summary of causes. The suggested interventions (napping, relaxation, sleep hygiene and a climatisation period) are not tested in the included studies, and the abstract states they 'could aid' performance without measuring performance.
paper.practicalImplications: The authors suggest timing travel to allow a settling period before competition, giving athletes psychological strategies for pre-competition nerves, and scheduling heavy training earlier in the day rather than late at night. These are suggestions drawn from associations, not tested interventions. Athletes with a concussion history reported more insomnia and short sleep, so sleep is worth asking about in that group.
paper.athleteDev: The review's introduction cites sleep loss linked to lower sprint performance and tennis accuracy, but the 16 included studies measured sleep rather than performance. Any performance effect of the travel, night-training and competition-night findings is therefore inferred from sleep outcomes alone.
paper.rtp: The review does not address return to sport. One included study linked insufficient sleep during recovery from sport-related concussion to more migraine, cognitive and neuropsychological symptoms, but the review gives no recovery timelines and cannot be used to decide when an athlete returns to play or training.

records.sourceFile: Chronotype, sleep hygiene, and sleep characteristics among athletes of different disciplines.pdf

paper.citation: Borghi S, Bizzozero S, Vitale JA, Tallini E, Corazza F, La Torre A, et al. Chronotype, sleep hygiene, and sleep characteristics among athletes of different disciplines. Int J Sports Med. 2024.
paper.abstract: This cross-sectional survey of 280 Italian athletes compared chronotype, sleep quality and sleep hygiene by sex, sport discipline (team or individual) and competition level (elite or non-elite). Nearly half the sample were poor sleepers by PSQI, and sleep hygiene correlated with both sleep quality and chronotype. The authors conclude that recovery and sleep deserve more attention from coaches.
paper.tldr: Many athletes in this Italian sample had weak sleep habits: 44.6% were poor sleepers by PSQI. Because the data are self-reported and cross-sectional, use the findings to flag athletes for sleep-habit screening rather than to set sport-specific sleep targets.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional online survey, reported to STROBE guidance, of athletes aged 18 to 40 who trained at least three times weekly during the 2022/2023 season. Participants completed the MEQ, the Italian PSQI, the Italian SHI and questions on training and ideal sleep. Non-normal data were compared with Mann-Whitney tests and correlated with Spearman tests.
paper.findings: Of 280 athletes, 66.4% were intermediate-type, 21.8% morning-type and 11.8% evening-type, and 44.6% were poor sleepers by PSQI. Females reported 14 minutes more total sleep than males (p = 0.022). Individual-sport athletes had lower PSQI (p = 0.006) and SHI (p < 0.001) scores, higher MEQ scores (p = 0.001) and a 36-minute earlier bedtime (p < 0.001) than team-sport athletes, and elite athletes reported higher sleep efficiency (+2.8%, p = 0.009), 2.1 minutes shorter latency (p = 0.018) and 11.3 minutes less WASO (p = 0.043) than non-elite athletes; all group effect sizes were small (about 0.25 to 0.51). PSQI correlated with SHI (r = 0.43) and MEQ with SHI (r = -0.35), both p < 0.001.
paper.limitations: Sleep was measured only by retrospective self-report, with possible recall bias, and naps, sleeping arrangements and second jobs were not controlled. The Discussion says team and individual athletes did not differ in quantitative or qualitative sleep parameters, but Table 2 shows PSQI, bedtime and wake-up time differed (total sleep time, efficiency, latency and WASO did not); the Results values are used here. The Discussion also says PSQI and MEQ were not correlated, while Figure 3 prints r = -0.23, p < 0.001, below the authors' r > 0.3 threshold.
paper.practicalImplications: Screening athletes with the PSQI and SHI may help staff identify who needs individual sleep-hygiene education, since poor sleep quality and poor sleep hygiene were linked in this sample. The study does not show that changing sleep hygiene improves sleep, so any intervention should be checked against the athlete's own sleep data.
paper.athleteDev: Team-sport athletes in this sample leaned later in chronotype and bedtime, which may be useful context when scheduling early sessions. The study does not measure performance, so it cannot show that any training time improves performance.
paper.rtp: This study does not include injured athletes or any return-to-sport outcome, so it cannot guide return-to-sport decisions. It is relevant only to general sleep-hygiene education for athletes who are not injured.
